themes.theme: Appraising whether AI is the right tool: benefits, alternatives, cost and pilots
themes.definition: Checks made before and around adoption on whether an AI tool is worth using compared with current systems or alternatives, including cost-benefit analysis, proofs of concept, pilots and tracking of benefits and running costs after deployment.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) tells bodies to evaluate the impact of an AI solution with tools such as cost-benefit analysis and to screen the use case against its principles for significant risks; UK099 asks teams to 'explain why AI is the right tool for this purpose'. UK268 is the most specific: comparative evaluation against current systems and feasible alternatives (historical comparisons, pilots, A/B testing per the coder note), a proof of concept for complex or high-cost projects, and indicators to track whether expected benefits are achieved after deployment. AI_Insights adds comparing candidate models against system objectives, close monitoring of running costs, and piloting on one or two drives before scaling; NAO commits itself to piloting AI and to 'begin measuring cost, performance and benefits'. UK082 calls for pilots with 'robust evaluation and publishing results', and UK266 asks audit committees whether pilot success criteria are scored and measured. No document says what size of benefit is enough, and none names who judges the result [inference: the judgement belongs to the Decision-making row].
themes.holders: 'You' (government departments and public sector organisations) in UK174 and UK099; not stated or 'the audited body' in UK268; NAO for its own use; KIM professionals and teams running generative AI in AI_Insights; the organisation answering audit committee questions in UK266.
themes.binding: Non-statutory throughout: recommended imperatives, 'should', 'can', questions, and NAO roadmap actions. No consequence for not doing it is stated anywhere.
themes.checks: Trigger: before use (cost-benefit analysis, proof of concept, pilot) and after deployment (benefit indicators, cost monitoring). Compared against: current systems, business-as-usual, feasible alternatives, system objectives, benefit targets. Metric or threshold: efficiency, accuracy, cost, performance, business impact; no thresholds. Who: mostly not stated; NAO for itself; KIM teams. What happens with the result: feeds the adoption decision [inference]; UK082 says pilot results should be published.

themes.theme: Setting requirements, metrics and thresholds before testing
themes.definition: Requirements that the yardstick for judging an AI tool (objectives, acceptance criteria, metrics and pass thresholds) be fixed in advance, so that later tests and monitoring have something to be compared against.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) says, with 'must', that bodies be clear about the 'objective measures' AI outputs are assessed against, and suggests user researchers and analysts define metrics for ongoing performance, but names no metric. UK268 expects traceability from objectives to 'model requirements that can be measured and monitored', an agreed quality assurance plan, and thresholds for acceptable performance and drift, all set by the organisation. UK071 is the only document that supplies worked numbers (a coder note records its example 'Validation accuracy = 92%, exceeding the 90% target') and asks that an initial risk classification set the depth of testing and the quality thresholds. AI_Insights says 'You must select the correct metrics' and that human reviewers test against benchmarks set during discovery; UK099 names fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalised odds) but leaves the choice to the team. The ATRS template (UK087) asks bodies to describe 'any performance thresholds your model should exceed', which records a threshold if one exists but does not require one. Across documents the act of choosing metrics is required or recommended, while the metrics and thresholds themselves are left to each deploying body [inference: so results are not comparable across bodies by design].
themes.holders: 'You' or the organisation; user researchers with analytical colleagues (UK174); teams (UK206, UK071); human reviewers (AI_Insights); the organisation completing the ATRS record (UK087); stakeholders (UK010, passive wording).
themes.binding: Mostly 'should' or imperatives in non-statutory guidance; 'must' in UK174 (017) and AI_Insights (433, 525), also non-statutory. The ATRS field is a required field under a policy that is mandatory for central government, but it does not oblige the body to have a threshold. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: project start, planning or discovery; before evaluation. Compared against: objectives, business requirements, 'clear performance benchmarks' (UK206), agreed benchmarks. Metric or threshold: left to the body; UK071 gives example metrics (accuracy, precision/recall, RMSE, F1) and example targets; UK099 names fairness metrics. Who: mostly not stated. What happens with the result: becomes the comparator for pre-deployment tests and monitoring; UK071 links thresholds to risk level.

themes.definition: Testing and evaluation of an AI tool before it goes live or is scaled up, including acceptance testing with users, operational readiness checks and testing whose depth is set by risk.
themes.what_is_set_out: Nearly every technical document asks for testing before use, in wording that runs from 'You should fully test the product before deployment' (UK174) to 'you must thoroughly test' before go-live (UK099) and 'it must be evaluated' against the standards in the project proposal (UK268, a non-prescriptive guide). UK268 and UK071 ask for testing under realistic conditions with end users in acceptance testing; UK071 adds an Operational Acceptance Test gate (covering, per the coder note, override, kill switches, undo and drift monitoring) and says high-risk AI demands 'exhaustive testing, possibly including formal verification or external audits before deployment'. UK010 (Ofgem) frames this as proportionate testing of the whole system, including its human and physical surroundings, and says rigorous testing 'is likely to be essential' before use. AI_Insights adds system and integration tests across execution paths for agentic systems, validation of user-built agents before they touch live data, and 'Every project must have an evaluation phase'; UK266 asks audit committees whether there is 'a robust, planned and resourced testing regime' when scaling from pilot to production. Depth is consistently tied to risk ('proportionate'), but no document sets a pass mark, and only the Secure by Design requirement in UK174 says outright that the service cannot be deployed until it is met.
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099); not stated, nearest the organisation (UK268); stakeholders and users of AI (UK010); the team, testers and project teams (UK071); 'we', system designers, entity creators and KIM teams (AI_Insights); the organisation answering audit committees (UK266).
themes.binding: Non-statutory throughout. Verbs range from 'can' and 'likely to be essential' (UK010) through 'should' to 'must' (UK099 before go-live; UK268; AI_Insights evaluation phase). The only stated consequence is that Secure by Design must be met 'before it can be deployed' (UK174, 067) [inference: a deployment gate]; UK071's Operational Acceptance Test is a 'should pass' gate.
themes.checks: Trigger: before deployment or go-live; before scaling from pilot; before an agent runs on live data. Compared against: standards in the project proposal, business indicators and acceptance criteria set at the start, 'all requirements set earlier in the project' (UK071 note), Secure by Design principles, system objectives. Metric or threshold: functional, performance, stress, adversarial and user acceptance tests; UK071 gives example targets (for instance end-to-end success of 95% or more); otherwise not stated. Who: mostly not stated; testers, end users in acceptance testing, KIM teams. What happens with the result: proceed to deployment; in AI_Insights' KIM guidance, return to development or redesign if benchmarks are not met (coder note to 501).

quotes.location: p. 35, Privacy: Test and validate
quotes.quote: Before going live with a new service, you must thoroughly test to ensure that it works as intended and does not introduce new privacy risks.

quotes.location: Continuous Defensive Assurance Model, Operational…

themes.theme: Checking output accuracy against a reference
themes.definition: Requirements to test or validate whether an AI tool's outputs are correct by comparing them with a reference, such as known good responses, ground truth, expert judgement, trusted sources, benchmarks or local data.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) asks bodies to 'establish accuracy measures', to test outputs 'against existing knowledge and expertise during training and testing', and says outputs 'should be tested against known good responses'; it also asks for validation checks so responses are accurate and do not leak data (coder note). UK268 expects outputs to be verified 'against trusted sources' to catch inaccuracies, performance evaluations using 'general benchmarks and application-specific tests', proportionate methods for detecting hallucinations, and, for bought-in systems, performance verified with local data; it also asks auditors to make sure that any AI used in the evaluation itself (such as an LLM acting as judge, per the coder note) has been evaluated by the project owner. UK071 names metrics (accuracy, precision/recall, RMSE, F1, BLEU/ROUGE, human ratings) and says testing should check 'whether it makes sense', not only whether it is correct. AI_Insights tells teams to validate outputs 'against ground truth or expert judgement', to evaluate RAG retrieval and generation separately, and to test LLM summaries for completeness and accuracy before relying on them; UK010 (Ofgem) suggests corroborating black-box output 'against known good data, research or expertise' and comparing AI models with traditional ones. NAO, UK206 and UK207 state accuracy as a principle, a benchmark comparison or a question without method, and no document gives an accuracy threshold for public-sector use: the reference, the metric and the pass mark are left to the body.
themes.holders: 'You' or the organisation and its teams; a sample of users (UK174, 005); the project owner for AI used in evaluation (UK268); KIM professionals and teams running generative AI (AI_Insights); NAO for itself; not stated in many passages.
themes.binding: Non-statutory: 'should', 'can', 'essential', 'may be necessary'. 'Must' appears in UK174 (017) and AI_Insights (433) without stated force. The one passage with a statutory link is UK174's statement that where AI systems infer data about people the system must be accurate (020, under data protection, placed in the data protection theme). No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: during training and testing; before deployment; before relying on outputs such as summaries; ongoing, especially on reuse or retraining (UK099, 260). Compared against: known good responses, existing knowledge and expertise, trusted sources, ground truth, expert judgement, general and application-specific benchmarks, local data, traditional models. Metric or threshold: accuracy, relevance, correctness, hallucination rate, precision/recall, F1, RMSE, BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR, share of sampled outputs rated acceptable; thresholds appear only as UK071 examples (for instance more than 80% of sampled outputs rated acceptable). Who: mostly not stated; users, human reviewers, evaluators. What happens with the result: mostly not stated; in AI_Insights' KIM guidance the solution is adjusted until it meets benchmarks.

themes.theme: Consistency, reproducibility and records of prompts, configuration and model versions
themes.definition: Checks that an AI tool gives stable outputs (for the same prompt, across environments and over time), and the records of prompts, generation settings, data and model versions needed to reproduce or audit its behaviour.
themes.what_is_set_out: Only UK268, AI_Insights and UK071 address this directly, with the ATRS adding model-identification fields. UK268 is the fullest: documenting prompt design and versioning and sampling parameters such as temperature and top-k (coder note) is 'essential for reproducibility', outputs should be tested for consistency by running the same prompt several times, version control should cover 'data, model artefacts, prompts, prediction outputs, and pipeline code', prompts and retrieval contexts should be tracked where full reproduction is impossible, and vendor and model versions in use should be tracked with regression tests after vendor updates. AI_Insights asks teams to 'test and measure to ensure consistency between environments' when development and production models differ, to keep data consistent across the range of acceptable inputs, to monitor prompt profiles for 'similar answers for similar questions over time', to version synthetic datasets, to monitor coding assistants' plugin and model versions and read their changelogs, and warns that a build pipeline 'should never rely on a specific response to a prompt' unless those responses are tested extensively. UK071 asks for dataset lineage logs linking data to model versions. The ATRS template and guidance (UK087, UK086) ask for the model type and, for pre-trained models, the API provider, with a related model-version field (coder note), but tell bodies to leave this section blank for off-the-shelf models they have not refined. No document sets a consistency threshold or says what should happen if repeated runs disagree.
themes.holders: Not stated in UK268 (expected controls; nearest the organisation); 'we' and developers in AI_Insights; the team in UK071; the organisation completing the ATRS record.
themes.binding: Non-statutory: UK268 'expected controls', 'essential', 'important'; AI_Insights uses 'must' (413, 415) with no stated force; ATRS fields are required under the ATRS policy but are disclosure, not a duty to test. No consequences stated beyond UK268's named risk that earlier production behaviour cannot be reproduced (coder note to 105).
themes.checks: Trigger: during development; after vendor updates; when development and production models differ; over time in use. Compared against: repeated runs of the same prompt; the other environment; earlier behaviour (regression); answers to similar questions over time. Metric or threshold: 'consistency' with no measure or threshold stated. Who: not stated. What happens with the result: not stated; UK268 links records to auditability and asks for fallback mechanisms when vendor updates cause regression.

themes.theme: Re-testing when the tool, model, data or context changes
themes.definition: Requirements to re-run tests or evaluations when an AI tool is updated, retrained, moved to another model or vendor version, fed new data, or used in a new context (split from the starting code 'testing').
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) states with 'must' that 'any updates to the AI system have a quantitative testing and validation process as part of the change control process', and that model updates go through a managed release. UK268 says retraining follows the same standards as first development, evaluation is repeated 'if the system or its environment changes', tests are rerun when monitoring exposes fairness, security or accuracy problems, and vendor updates trigger regression testing. UK071 asks for procedures 'to retest models whenever they change' and for fairness checks to be rerun on change, with periodic retesting on recent data (for example quarterly). AI_Insights is the most emphatic about model swaps: if an agent's underlying LLM changes, 'extensive testing must be undertaken'; profiling and attack-surface testing are 'mandatory prior to any model change'; tests run on small development models must be rerun on larger deployed ones; and new versions of packages or models 'require re-affirmation of safeguards'. UK133 asks for further impact evaluation when a tool is applied to a new context or changed significantly, and UK099 for review at milestones and significant updates. The trigger is stated clearly here, unusually for this cell, but what counts as a significant change, what the re-test must show and who accepts the result are not stated.
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099); not stated (UK268, UK071); 'we', system designers and teams (AI_Insights); evaluators (UK133).
themes.binding: 'Must' in UK174 (054) and AI_Insights (423; 437 'mandatory') in non-statutory guidance; 'should' elsewhere. UK268 names the risk that the behaviour of earlier production versions cannot be reproduced (coder note to 105). No sanctions.
themes.checks: Trigger: updates, retraining, fine-tuning, vendor or model version changes, a change of underlying LLM, new data, pipeline changes, a new context, detected drift, issues found in monitoring, milestones. Compared against: previous behaviour (regression), the original standards and acceptance criteria, requirements for intended use (coder note to 054). Metric or threshold: 'quantitative' but unspecified; UK071 gives an example re-test success rate of 95% or more (coder note to 349). Who: not stated. What happens with the result: managed release with documented changes; fallback mechanisms; retraining policies; re-affirmed safeguards.

quotes.quote: You must ensure that any updates to the AI system have a quantitative testing and validation process as part of the change control process.

themes.theme: Ongoing monitoring of performance, drift and harms in live use
themes.definition: Continuing checks on an AI tool once it is in use, covering accuracy, drift, bias, harmful outputs, costs and whether it still does what it was designed to do.
themes.what_is_set_out: Monitoring is asked for by almost every document, usually with 'should': ongoing performance monitoring with the ability to 'provide evidence of this' (UK174); continuous tracking of accuracy, reliability, robustness and key performance indicators set during planning, with automated drift checks and thresholds the organisation defines (UK268); and comparing real-world outcomes against model predictions with alerts (UK071). UK010 (Ofgem) suggests independent comparators such as digital twins or conventional systems (coder note); the EHRC checklist (UK216) treats the Public Sector Equality Duty as an 'ongoing duty' that is 'likely to include' regular monitoring of whether people with protected characteristics are treated differently; UK136 says ongoing testing is needed to maintain accuracy and that the department should agree with the supplier how efficacy will be monitored. AI_Insights adds production profiling of expected against achieved performance, monitoring of agent iterations and of costs, and the strongest wording in the theme: 'All communicated data must be monitored and evaluated without exception.' UK099 and UK071 extend monitoring to societal impact, such as rising complaint rates or disproportionate effects on marginalised groups. Monitoring is rarely tied to a consequence: UK268 asks for evaluation tests to be rerun and retraining policies to be set when drift is detected, but who decides and which threshold triggers action are left to the body.
themes.holders: 'You', the organisation or its team; business owners to be kept aware of performance (UK268); public bodies (UK216); stakeholders (UK010); teams and operational teams (UK071); NAO for itself; central government departments with suppliers (UK136); organisation completing ATRS (UK087).
themes.binding: Non-statutory and mostly 'should' or 'can'. 'Must' in UK071 (325, in a non-mandatory framework) and AI_Insights (488) without stated force. The EHRC places ongoing monitoring within a statutory duty (the PSED), but the monitoring method is its interpretation ('likely to include'). No sanctions stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: ongoing or continuous after deployment; scheduled (UK071's example of quarterly retesting); post-implementation. Compared against: KPIs set at planning, expected operation, real-world outcomes against predictions, historical ranges, other groups (PSED), independent comparator systems. Metric or threshold: accuracy, drift, bias, hallucinations, latency and error rates, cost, complaint rates; thresholds are to be 'defined' by the body (UK268) and appear only as examples in UK071. Who: mostly not stated; teams; business owners informed. What happens with the result: rerun evaluation tests, retrain, raise alerts; UK099 asks whether a system no longer serving its purpose can be decommissioned.

themes.theme: Bias and fairness testing across groups
themes.definition: Testing and review of whether an AI tool's outputs or performance differ unfairly between groups, including protected and intersectional groups, and mitigation where bias is found (split from the starting code 'evaluation').
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) asks for measurements of output accuracy and quality against the protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010 and for review 'for different groups of people including intersectional groups', and says with 'must' that fairness be ensured to comply with legal and human rights requirements. UK268 describes counterfactual testing (changing gender or location in the input and checking whether outputs change), benchmark datasets across groups, a warning against relying on a single fairness metric (coder note), and a duty on the buyer to check that a developer's fairness tests are relevant to the intended use. UK099 asks teams to work out which aspects of fairness matter (for example equal error rates between groups when flagging fraudulent claims, per the coder note), to choose fairness metrics, to review data and models for proxies, and, with 'must', to mitigate bias once it is found. UK071 gives the most operational version: test outputs 'separately by group', with example thresholds (a demographic parity gap of 10% or less; accuracy within ±5%, per the coder note), prompt templates that differ only by demographic markers, reruns on change, and review of results by both technical and policy/legal teams. UK010 (Ofgem), UK139 (regulators) and UK136 (procurement) ask regulated firms, developers and deployers, or suppliers to identify and mitigate bias, and AI_Insights notes that coding assistants will not flag bias, leaving it to the developer. Wording ranges from 'can' to 'must', and thresholds appear only as examples in UK071.
themes.holders: 'You' or the organisation; teams; technical and policy/legal teams (UK071); the auditee organisation for third-party models (UK268); evaluators (UK133); stakeholders (UK010); AI developers and deployers within regulators' remits (UK139); developers (AI_Insights); tender evaluators and suppliers (UK136).
themes.binding: Non-statutory guidance, though several passages tie it to the Equality Act 2010 or the PSED (UK174, UK099, UK071). 'Must' in UK174 (042), UK099 (237) and UK010 (287, with no basis cited at that point). No sanctions stated; UK099 warns that unfairness may result in unlawful discrimination (coder note to 234).
themes.checks: Trigger: during development; on any change to models or rules (UK071); ongoing in live operation (UK268, UK099); not stated in many passages. Compared against: other groups; counterfactual versions of the same input; benchmark datasets; equality law; the intended use case and data. Metric or threshold: performance and error rates by group, demographic parity, equalised odds, change in output under counterfactual inputs; numeric thresholds only as UK071 examples. Who: mostly not stated; UK071 has technical and policy/legal teams review results. What happens with the result: mitigation is required once bias is identified (UK099); fairness metrics and rationale are documented (UK268).

themes.theme: Risk-tiered bias controls for generative AI (LLMs)
themes.definition: A graded scheme, set out in one AI_Insights article on LLM bias, that assigns an LLM application a bias risk level from its context and then requires escalating mitigations, evaluations, deployment gates, production monitoring and human review at each level.
themes.what_is_set_out: This is the only place in the UK cell where the depth of checking AI outputs is tied to explicit triggers. A three-step risk assessment asks whether output influences protected-class decisions (start at High), is public-facing (High), reaches external users (Medium) or is internal only (Low), and raises the level by one step when escalation triggers apply, such as age, socioeconomic or political content. The resulting table labels both mitigations and evaluations 'Required': Low needs a 'Pre-deployment bias check' and user feedback monitoring; Medium adds 'Monthly automated testing' and 'Human review for edge cases'; High adds a counterfactual testing suite, real-time bias alerting and continuous production monitoring; Critical adds red-team testing, a complete audit trail and a 'Per-release bias impact assessment'. The integration pipeline should treat bias evaluation as 'a mandatory gate' that blocks deployments exceeding predefined thresholds regardless of gains elsewhere; in production, traffic is sampled at rates that scale with risk, statistical process control separates normal variation from drift, and outputs in ambiguous classifier ranges or sensitive areas 'can be routed to trained reviewers'. Each incident should be recorded with the triggering metrics, response, root cause and preventive measures. The thresholds themselves are not given, holders are mostly not stated (nearest: engineering teams), and the whole scheme sits in non-binding guidance.
themes.holders: Not stated; nearest named actors are engineering teams and developers; trained reviewers for routed cases; human evaluation panels at the higher levels (coder notes).
themes.binding: Non-binding guidance. Verbs: 'should', 'must' (bias management 'must be embedded at every stage', 453), and table cells labelled 'Required'. The only stated consequence is that the integration gate blocks deployment when thresholds are exceeded (533).
themes.checks: Trigger: pre-commit hooks, every merge to main, staging before production, each release (Critical), monthly (Medium), continuously (High and Critical). Compared against: predefined thresholds; historical ranges through control charts; counterfactual prompt pairs. Metric or threshold: bias metrics and classifier scores, not specified; sampling rates scale with risk; thresholds are 'predefined' but not given. Who: not stated; trained reviewers for ambiguous or sensitive outputs. What happens with the result: deployment blocked; alerts; actionable reports naming failure modes and remediation paths; incident records for post-incident review.
